toolCalls.name: StructuredOutput

output.methodChoice: Collected 2 of 2 items. X15 first: it compares night and day shifts and suppliers, which tests the staffing-cut explanation directly. Then X13: independent trailer logs, to test whether Haverlow loads arrived warm. I skipped the credit-side items because they affect only about 15% of the rise and would not change the lead action.
output.brief:
Most of the jump comes from inside the DC, not from Haverlow. Since the night receiving team was cut from six to four on 27 July, night-received chilled pallets wait a median 3h52 (previously 44 minutes) on an unrefrigerated dock averaging 15–17°C before reaching the chambers. Night write-offs rose from 0.6% to 2.9%; day shift stayed near 0.5%; the night rate is the same for Haverlow, Pellridge and own-label. The trailers' own uneditable logs show Haverlow product at 2.4–3.5°C when doors opened; the 'warm' receipt probes were recorded about 3.5 hours after unloading. Chambers held temperature. DC-stage write-offs are up about £15,700 a week against a £2,300 weekly labour saving.

I'm about 90% sure. Less certain is the £2,700 weekly rise in customer credits: Corriebank's easier claims may explain some, real dock-delay spoilage may explain the rest; the evidence can't yet split them.

Next: restore the night team, set a maximum dock-to-chamber time, and track it weekly from scan data. Suspend the Haverlow chargeback and volume move; keep the receiving probe. Separately, get Corriebank's claim-level data and check a sample before changing credit terms.
